The 2024 data of the Philippine Statistics Authority showed that the BARMM had the lowest basic literacy rate among all regions in the country at 81 percent. Lanao del Sur ranked third among the region’s five provinces.







MARAWI CITY, Lanao del Sur — Affecting one’s education due to financial difficulties is a typical problem of poor communities in many parts of the country. But for families displaced after the Marawi Siege in 2017, having such a problem amid their continuing displacement hits differently.




There were many occasions that the children of Nurania Unte, 33, were not able to go to school due to financial constraints. Her family is now living in Hijrah village, Barangay Sultan Corobong, a remote temporary shelter in the Islamic City of Marawi.

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: After joining protests, Ayta leader faces military harassment
content:
An Ayta community leader in Zambales faced military interrogation and surveillance days after joining protests against the US-backed Pax Silica initiative, raising concerns over the harassment of Indigenous Peoples defending their ancestral lands.

Orlino Lahut, also known as Tiyong Nilo, was visited by a military personnel identifying himself as Jasper Dalit in the afternoon of November 19 at the residence of an Ayta community elder in Iram, Zambales.

According to statements from Indigenous Peoples’ and environmental organizations, Dalit questioned Lahut about the community’s recent trip to Manila, including who organized their participation in the protests, who provided their “Reject Pax Silica” shirts, and how they financed their transportation.

Lahut was also reportedly coerced into completing a form requiring his personal information and organizational affiliations. Dalit threatened to return with additional personnel to question other community members.

The incident followed reports that unidentified men in civilian clothing monitored Ayta delegates during their journey home from Manila.

Katribu Youth Katipunan, Amihan National Federation of Peasant Women, and Kalikasan People’s Network for the Environment condemned the incident, describing it as an attempt to intimidate Indigenous communities exercising their right to protest.

Lahut rejected claims that the Ayta were manipulated by outsiders, asserting that their participation in the demonstrations was based on their own decision and opposition to projects threatening their ancestral domains. “We are not fools,” he said.

For the Ayta communities in Central Luzon, opposition to Pax Silica is premised on the threat to their ancestral lands, livelihoods, and environment.

The initiative, alongside the Marcos Jr. administration’s Luzon Economic Corridor, includes proposed developments such as the Aboitiz solar power project in Olongapo and an artificial intelligence and semiconductor hub in New Clark City, Tarlac.

These developments threaten ancestral and agricultural lands, including areas containing Ayta burial grounds. Amihan also warned that affected communities could face relocation to areas without adequate livelihood opportunities and access to clean water.

The proposed data hub is projected to consume up to 1.8 billion gallons of water annually and operate around the clock, with noise levels potentially reaching 105 decibels, according to Amihan.

Zenaida Soriano, national chairperson of Amihan, said that the initiative would further expose the country’s natural resources to foreign exploitation at the expense of Indigenous communities and farmers. “Pax Silica is a project of wealthy countries that will only destroy our lands, waters, and Indigenous communities.”

She stressed that the developments also threaten national food security, particularly with the planned expansion of the Luzon Economic Corridor across major ports in Luzon.

The harassment of Lahut coincided with another attack against an environmental defender, Lumad youth activist Mawing Pangadas, coordinator of Panalipdan Youth Davao. He was pursued by 10 to 12 suspected state agents wearing black clothing and caps along Upper Madapo Hills in Barangay 8-A, Davao City.

Read: Groups decry abduction attempt on Lumad youth activist in Davao City

Kalikasan condemned both incidents, stressing that these are growing threats against environmental defenders who oppose destructive projects and protect their communities’ land and resources.

For 13 consecutive years, the Philippines has been Asia’s deadliest country for environmental defenders, according to environmental organizations.

Despite this record, the Marcos Jr. administration has proposed a P9.75-billion ($152 million) budget for the National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC) in 2027, nearly P2 billion ($31 million) higher than its previous allocation.

Kalikasan criticized the proposed allocation, saying it results in sustained red-tagging, surveillance, and militarization instead of addressing the needs of communities affected by land grabbing and environmental destruction.

Soriano also condemned the continued military presence in rural communities, saying intimidation would not stop farmers and Indigenous Peoples from defending their rights. “Marcos and the military serve their master Donald Trump rather than the Filipino people. They resort to violence and intimidation to seize land and sell it to foreign businesses.”

The organizations called for an investigation into the attempted abduction of Pangadas and the prosecution of those responsible. They also demanded an end to the surveillance and harassment of Lahut and other Ayta leaders, as well as the withdrawal of military personnel from their communities.

Amihan vowed to continue opposing the exploitation of the country’s natural resources and the militarization of rural communities. (AMU, DAA)

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: ‘Predators-in-chief’ attack ICC
content:
Former United Nations (UN) Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial killing Agnès Callamard visited the Philippines after almost a decade of being barred from entering the country.

“It begins with Duterte, in a few weeks. But it doesn’t end there,” said Callamard, also Amnesty International’s secretary-general in a press conference on November 20. “This is bigger than him. It is about the Philippines. It’s about humanity.”

When she was UN Special Rapporteur, she called for investigations into the thousands of killings under Duterte’s anti-illegal drugs campaign. The immigration ban started in 2017 and Duterte ordered that she and any representatives of the International Criminal Court (ICC) be arrested and deported.

Callamard’s immigration ban was lifted in September 2026 after years of petitioning the Philippine authorities, with the support of Amnesty International Philippines and support from several lawmakers.

“The supposed war on drugs was a slaughter that destroyed lives and families. They have carried their grief with little hope for justice and nowhere else to turn for almost a decade,” Callamard said.

Duterte is charged with three counts of crimes against humanity by the ICC for extrajudicial killings during his term as Davao City mayor and President of the Philippines. His trial is set to begin on November 30.

Human rights organizations reported more than 30,000 extrajudicial killing victims from Duterte’s anti-illegal drugs campaign, significantly higher than the official government records of just over 6,000 victims. Only five cases resulted in conviction and some of them remain on appeal.

“We had conversations with the victims, survivors, and families in the past 48 hours [with Callamard]. It is still depressing. The families have accepted that there will be no justice at home and that they are depending on what will happen in The Hague. It is very ironic,” said Ritz Lee Santos III, section director of Amnesty International Philippines. “We have a justice system here at home. The government is claiming that they are working, but the victims’ families are saying that there is no hope. There is still a culture of impunity and a climate of fear.”

These structures, both of them said, are evident in the continuing drug-related extrajudicial killings, Duterte’s children remaining in power, and the widespread vilification of the victims and their families.

Read: Women human rights defenders face rising tech-assisted violence

The United States has imposed sanctions against the ICC, banning transactions with the court to paralyze its resources and ability to operate. The administration of US President Donald Trump previously sanctioned 13 prosecutors and judges of the ICC, three Palestinian human rights organizations, and the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory Francesca Albanese.

Read: US intensifies sanctions vs. ICC

The United States, China, and Russia issued a so-called “peace declaration” in their first trilateral summit on November 29, after Trump’s visit in Manila, Philippines. Particularly, the ICC garnered special attention in their declaration.

“The three heads of state recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction,” the declaration read.

Part of the declaration is to “reform” the United Nations (UN) as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC).

“They are the ‘predators-in-chief’ in our current system. This so-called peace treaty is about as worthless as who they are– predators,” said Callamard, highlighting their aggression in Venezuela, Iran, and Palestine. “They are attacking the ICC because international justice for them is a battle ground.”

“We are calling on the rest of the world to stand up to these predatory actions and threats. There are far more governments that ratified the Rome Statute. So in terms of the numbers, we are far more powerful than they are,” Callamard said.

In her international human rights work, Callamard said that there are less powerful governments living in fear of what the US, Russia, and China could do in their economy. “It is about economic characters being fearful of being kept out of the American market, Russian market, or the China market. And for those reasons, humanity is being thrown out. We’re being hanged, sold in fact. The soul of our work, of our humanity, is being sold so that some rich individuals can make a few bucks on those markets.”

She called on ICC member-states to push back against the sanctions. “They have the legal, political, and policy tools to push back. But they haven’t done that. The problem is not just the predators-in-chief, but also the cowards.”

During the press conference, she also led the launching of Walang Pahimakas (No Farewell: Anthology of Poems on the “War on Drugs”) published this year by Amnesty International Philippines. It is a collection of poems that brings stories of the victims and their families at the forefront of the search for justice, accountability, and truth.

“In a climate marked by fear and silencing critics, the written word becomes a means of restoring the truth. Walang Pahimakas is an act of remembering lives that were reduced to labels and statistics,” editor and poet Ron Atilano said. “Poetry cannot bring back those who were killed nor can it take away the trauma of losing a loved one in cold-blooded murder, but it refuses to let lives be forgotten. These poems remind us that behind every reported killing was a human being, and behind every victim was a family whose lives were forever changed.” (RTS, DAA)

author: Dulce Amor Rodriguez
title: Filipino migrant healthcare workers denounce ICE detention, deportation threats
content:
Image of packaged sent to Balllesteros (photo from CLSU USSC)

Filipino migrant healthcare workers condemned the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown while raising concerns over medical neglect inside US detention facilities.

Speaking at a press conference organized by Tanggol Migrante Movement USA on November 13, two Filipino healthcare workers called for humane treatment and due process for migrants, regardless of their immigration status or profession.

Mariae “LC” Nacu was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Phoenix, Arizona, on August 22.

The 22-year-old registered nurse had been working at St. Joseph’s Hospital in Phoenix and has a valid employment authorization.

She was held at the Eloy Detention Center for three weeks before her release on bond, according to Tanggol Migrante Movement USA.

The organization said that her bond was set at $17,000 (P1.08 million) on November 13.

Nacu also estimated that she spent around $300 weekly (P19,068) on commissary items and phone calls while detained.

More than two months after her detention, ICE continued to hold her identification documents, including her driver’s license, according to the organization.

“The difficult part was that I wasn’t there [in the detention center] as a nurse. I was another person in detention, locked in a cell, trying to get someone to listen,” Nacu said.

She recalled witnessing a medical emergency involving another detainee and struggling to get someone to listen to her concerns.

Nacu described the separation from loved ones, handcuffing, and transfers between detention facilities without knowing where she was going as “traumatizing and dehumanizing.”

Dr. Veronica Velasquez, a Filipino physical therapist and recipient of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), faces the threat of being deported.

Co-chair of the Los Angeles Kalusugan Collective, Velasquez regularly visits detainees at the Adelanto Detention Center where she witnessed brutality and medical neglect.

Velasquez said that she has organized with Tanggol Migrante Movement USA for two years and continues to support detained migrants despite facing immigration-related uncertainty herself. “I am a healthcare worker who has seen firsthand the brutality inside detention centers. I, myself, am threatened with deportation and have experienced over 23 years of this immigrant injustice system. Even so, I’m here still fighting for my community while the community fights for me.”

She said that nearly 100 community members attended her first court hearing.

Both healthcare workers raised concerns about the treatment of migrants inside US detention facilities, particularly their access to medical attention.

Velasquez said that her experience in visiting detainees exposed her to cases of alleged brutality and medical neglect. “As healthcare workers, we are in a special position to shed light on these issues of migrants in detention […] You cannot deny us from saying that there is medical violence happening in these detention centers.”

Nacu’s account of witnessing another detainee’s medical emergency also underscored the difficulties people in detention face when seeking help.

Her testimony, however, does not independently establish the circumstances or outcome of the medical emergency.

Bulatlat previously reported the case of a Filipino detainee, Kuya G, who underwent a toe amputation after months of alleged medical neglect at the Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma, Washington.

Migrant rights advocates said that detention facility personnel failed to properly diagnose and address his condition.

The case adds to concerns raised by migrant organizations about the treatment and medical care available to people held in immigration detention.

Read: Filipino migrants face inhumane treatment at ICE detention centers

Velasquez raised concerns over the slow response and lack of accountability of Philippine consulates who are supposed to be assisting detained migrants. She cited one case where a consulate called the police on mothers of detainees who were seeking assistance.

Her remarks echo concerns raised by Filipino migrant organizations about the Philippine government’s response to the detention of Filipino nationals in the United States.

Nacu said that access to humane treatment, medical care, and due process should not depend on a person’s profession or immigration status. “We shouldn’t have to be nurses, doctors, or healthcare workers to deserve dignity. Every person deserves humane treatment, necessary medical care, and due process, regardless of their profession or immigration status.”

The two healthcare workers called for solidarity with migrants facing detention and deportation threats. “In nursing, when someone needs help, we don’t expect one person to handle everything alone. We communicate, support each other, and work as a team. I hope we can bring that same commitment to the people and communities affected by immigration detention,” Nacu said. (RTS, DAA)

title: Eastern Visayas farmers suffer from El Niño
content:
TACLOBAN CITY – “All the crops I planted, even if they are supposed to withstand heat, all died because of the extreme drought caused by the El Niño.”

Gil Gacus, a farmer from Samar, stressed this point at the October 28 forum at the University of the Philippines Tacloban titled “Istorya Pankalibungan: A Forum on Climate Change and Environmental Challenges.”

The event was attended by members of organizations of fisherfolk and farmers, environmental defenders, development workers from Leyte and Samar, youth groups, and students from different universities in Tacloban. Farmers from Magsasaka at Siyentipiko para sa Pag-unlad ng Agrikultura (MASIPAG) shared the impact of Super El Niño on their crops.

Gacus said that the lack of a reliable irrigation system adds up to farmers’ burdens. “We have irrigation canals but there is little to no water due to drought so our crops end up dying.”

Jeremias Maligmat, a farmer from Leyte, stressed the need for government action now that farmers are suffering from the effects of El Niño. He also criticized Marcos Jr.’s lack of urgency and genuineness to help them. “He [Marcos Jr.] is asking us to use pails to collect rainwater, but how will we collect it if there is no rain?”

“If Marcos is genuine about helping farmers, his government should focus on addressing the challenges on irrigation and invest in machinery that could pump out underground water to help us farmers during times like this,” Maligmat said.

Maligmat added that on top of the environmental challenges and outright neglect from the government, landlessness is also a major problem faced by farmers. “The government should address these challenges affecting us farmers if they are so genuine about helping us as we are the ones producing food for the country.”

Roque Regis of Save Kanbatok Advocacy criticized the government’s reaffirmation to continue the halted construction of the Causeway Project in Cancabato Bay. “Since the construction of the Causeway started last 2023, there have already been recorded, irreversible damages to the bay. It destroyed the then thriving ecosystem of the bay by obstructing the natural flow of water.”

Regis said that some of his fellow fisherfolk have stopped from fishing due to the deteriorating state of the Bay. “These so-called developmental projects like the causeway project do not benefit the community or the poor, but instead benefit the rich who embezzle money through these projects.”

“Fisherfolk like Mano Roque struggled heavily, so much so that the fish, crabs, and other seafood they catch, if they have any at all, shrunk in size over the years since land was dumped on Cancabato Bay to build that Causeway,” said Jerx Aliposa of Save Kankabato Advocacy.

“Instead of coming up with solutions to address their concerns like providing subsidies and investing on technologies that could help them, the government would always think of developmental projects like the causeway project, with little to no regard of their repercussions to our communities,” Aliposa said.

Nemesio Baldesco of Tinambacan Environmental Advocates Coalition (TEAC), a network of environmental defenders from Calbayog City in Samar, said that their group opposes the Gemini Wind Power Project by Vena Energy in their city. “[I]t will greatly affect the biodiversity of our forests and will pollute our sources of clean water.”

Although their group and other advocates succeeded in getting at least five wind turbines removed from Pan-as Hayiban watershed, Calbayog’s protected landscape, Nemesio said that the project is yet to be abandoned. “Their [Vena Energy] alternative route is to install the turbines outside the watershed but still within our forests where it could still disrupt the biodiversity and result in the cutting down of hundreds of trees.”

WATCH : Envi advocates oppose Gemini Wind Project in Samar

Ronnel Arambulo, Vice Chairperson of Pambansang Lakas ng Kilusang Mamamalakaya ng Pilipinas (PAMALAKAYA), stressed the importance of collective action as well as the youth’s participation to oppose projects that damage the environment and livelihoods of farmers and fisherfolks. “Let us not allow our schools to become producers of brains that will only be used by the rich to forward their anti-poor agenda.” Ronnie Manalo, secretary-general of the Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP), called on the farmers to fight for their rightful claim on the P45-billion funds allocated for El Niño. “Let us mobilize our farmers to compute all their losses and damages due to El Niño and collectively submit petitions to government agencies like the Department of Agriculture and our respective local government units.”

Jasmin Aguisanda-Jerusalem of Leyte Center for Development and Empowerment (LCDE), linked the challenges of our farmers and fisherfolks to our country’s economic policies. “Our economy is import-dependent when we have our local producers. It is clear that the policies we have in place are all for the profit of the few.” As a development worker for 45 years, Jerusalem witnessed the dire economic and political conditions of people in Eastern Visayas. “Despite helping almost 800,000 people since LCDE started in 1988, we were slapped with criminal cases all because we decided to help those who are in need.”

“A strong people’s movement deeply rooted in communities–in schools, farms, factories–is what we need to change the very system [that] is rotten to the core,” Jerusalem said. (RTS, DAA)

author: Maverick Avila
title: 3 UN experts press the Philippines over mass detentions of ASEAN summit protesters
content:
Three United Nations Special Rapporteurs have publicly called out the Philippine government over the reported detention of more than 300 people during protests at the opening of the ASEAN 2026 summit, warning that the arrests point to a broader squeeze on dissent.

The mass arrest happened last November 15, 2026 when demonstrations broke out across Metro Manila to coincide with the regional summit to oppose the U.S.-led Pax technology and mining initiative and the presence of U.S. President Donald Trump. They were released on the night of November 18, following a decision of the Muntinlupa prosecutor.

Read: Police violently disperse, arrest hundreds in Muntinlupa protest

Among the arrested are mostly members of the Southern Tagalog group Lakbayan in Muntinlupa City, alongside media workers including student journalists, and progressive groups at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila, and Bulacan.

Andrea Bolaños Vargas, Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights defenders, said she is concerned by reports of police violence against peaceful protesters and is monitoring the safety and protection of human rights defenders.

?? I am concerned by reports of police violence against peaceful protesters and arrests in the ?? #Philippines amid #ASEAN2026. I have received worrying information about the situation and am closely monitoring developments, including regarding the safety and protection of human…

“I have received worrying information about the situation and am closely monitoring developments, including regarding the safety and protection of human rights defenders,” Vargas said.

Gina Romero, UN Special Rapporteur on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and of association, wrote she received reports that security officials earlier in the week urged groups to hold off on protests until after the summit, reportedly to avoid a bad image before foreign visitors.

#Philipines today's police behaviour mirror a wider crackdown on dissent in the country. I have been receiving worrisome information about sedition subpoenas for anti-corruption protests, authorities tagging student leaders as "wanted", military home visits & campus lockdowns 3/

“Peaceful protests are not a PR question, they are a (human rights) issue,”

Romero added that this goes beyond the image of the ASEAN Summit taking place in the country. “(The) Philippines prior protests on related issues such as the pax silica have also been harassed,” she wrote.

Astrid Riano, Special Rapporteur on the right to a clean, safe and healthy environment, also said she is closely following the situation in Manila and in demonstrations elsewhere in the country.

Read: ‘Make Pax Silica deal public’

Riano also emphasized that ASEAN’s efforts should be aligned on its declaration to the right of a safe, clean, healthy, and sustainable environment at the 47th ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur on October 26, 2025. This declaration aimed to address climate change, biodiversity loss, and environmental pollution.

“The right to a #healthyenvironment includes access to information and public participation, which includes peaceful demonstrations,” Riano said.

The same police brutality during Anti-Pax Silica protests are also prevalent across the regions of the country.

WATCH: https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1M2RrsZA81/

In Cebu City, rights group Karapatan Central Visayas has recorded reports of at least 10 attempted arrests and about 20 people injured in the police dispersal, with one protester reportedly rushed to the emergency room.

On November 18, 2026, the arrested protesters were released after three days in detention. Global civil society alliance CIVICUS is urging the Philippine government to investigate police restrictions and excessive force against protesters during the ASEAN Summit in Manila. (RVO)

author: Josiah David Quising
title: Legality of burning effigies
content:
Throughout history, the burning of effigies was never shown to be with intent to injure another, but rather consistently presented as a form of expression and indignation.

Filipinos using effigies to depict resistance and protest is said to have originated from the higantes of Angono, Rizal as a way to mock abusive hacenderos in the late Spanish colonial period. Decades later, Filipino activists have kept the tradition alive across multiple administrations, but not without opposition. The Philippine National Police (PNP) often releases warnings against burning effigies ahead of protests, claiming that burning protest materials would violate either the Republic Act No. 8749 (Clean Air Act) or Batas Pambansa No. 880 (Public Assembly Act). Just yesterday, Cebu activists were accused by the local police of violating the law when they set an effigy on fire.

But does burning effigies really violate the law? The PNP has cited Section 20 of the Philippine Clean Air Act which bans incineration of “municipal, biomedical, and hazardous waste” as the basis of their warning, stating that burning effigies would pollute the air.

A plain reading of the law would show that the ban on incineration does not prohibit all types of burning but instead specifically prohibits the burning of “waste”. While the Clean Air Act itself does not define “waste”, Section 3(kk) of R.A. 9003 or the Solid Waste Management Act defines “solid waste” as “all discarded household, commercial waste, non-hazardous institutional and industrial waste, street sweepings, construction debris, agricultural waste, and other non-hazardous/non-toxic solid waste.”

By plain definition, effigies cannot be categorized as “waste” as they are not “discarded” materials but rather art forms created for a specific purpose. The Supreme Court clarified this in MMDA v. Jancom (2002) where it held that Section 20 of the Philippine Clean Air Act does not absolutely prohibit incineration. It prohibits only burning processes involving municipal, biomedical, or hazardous wastes that emit poisonous and toxic fumes. This means that even in the absurd scenario where effigies are considered as “waste” materials, burning of the same would still not be considered a violation of the Philippine Clean Air Act.

“Poisonous and toxic fumes” are defined by Section 5(t) of the Clean Air Act as “any emissions and fumes which are beyond internationally-accepted standards, including but not limited to the World Health Organization (WHO) guideline values.”

This shows that without proof that the burning of effigies during protests would result in emissions of fumes “beyond internationally-accepted standards,” burning of effigies does not automatically violate the Philippine Clean Air Act.

Another law commonly cited by the PNP is Section 13(g)(3) of the Public Assembly Act which prohibits the “malicious burning of any object in the streets or thoroughfares”. The Supreme Court in Villareal v. People (2012) has defined “malice” or “malicious” as the deliberate, wrongful, or evil intent to injure another, or an act done with criminal indifference to another’s rights and without legal justification.

In other words, the intent or reason for the burning matters. Throughout history, the burning of effigies was never shown to be with intent to injure another, but rather consistently presented as a form of expression and indignation.

Ultimately, no law directly prohibits the burning of effigies. The PNP should stop distracting everyone from the issues brought to light by setting fire to art. At the end of the day, the government should address the message itself rather than fixate on how it was delivered – perhaps then we can return to calmly submitting position papers. (DAA)

title: Faith groups stand with detained protesters
content:
Police arrest protesters, including members of alternative media and student publications, in Sucat, Muntinlupa City, on November 15, 2026. The protesters are part of a delegation who are set to join a protest in Manila against Pax Silica and US President Donald Trump's visit. Photo from Bayan Laguna

“What we are fighting for is engagement and trade grounded in equality, respect for sovereignty, and mutual benefit.”

Ecumenical councils, Christian youth, and Catholic bishops denounce the US-led critical minerals deal and state crackdown ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit.

More than 300 protesters were detained at Camp Bagong Diwa of the Philippine National Police in Taguig City following aggressive police dispersals on November 15. Police dispersed the Southern Tagalog Lakbayan protest caravan in Sucat, Parañaque and Muntinlupa while separate clashes happened at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila.

The protests targeted the proposed signing of the Pax Silica framework during US President Donald Trump’s visit to Manila. Meanwhile, Protestant, ecumenical, and Roman Catholic leaders warned that they will sacrifice Philippine sovereignty, ancestral lands, and public utilities to US geopolitical and corporate interests.

In a pastoral statement issued Nov. 12, 2026, the National Council of Churches in the Philippines (NCCP) condemned both the economic terms of Pax Silica and the Marcos Jr. administration’s suppression of constitutionally guaranteed freedoms. “In a display of servility to the US, the government of Pres. Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is rolling out the red carpet, spending billions of pesos on lavish preparations while ordinary Filipinos struggle with poverty, rising prices, and economic hardship. In true ‘Imeldific’ fashion, authorities are clearing Manila’s streets of vendors and urban poor communities to conceal poverty from visiting dignitaries. Worse, they have imposed a ban on protests, suppressing constitutionally guaranteed freedoms.”

Signed by NCCP Chairperson The Most Rev. Brent Harry W. Alawas and General Secretary Minnie Anne Mata-Calub, the statement warned that Pax Silica’s push for critical minerals, semiconductor supply chains and artificial intelligence data centers places the country squarely in the crosshairs of superpower conflict. “More alarming is the prospect of signing the lopsided Pax Silica agreement during Trump’s visit. Designed to secure US access to critical technology supply chains, including artificial intelligence and critical minerals, the agreement places Philippine resources and sovereignty at the service of US strategic interests amid its rivalry with China. Pax Silica threatens to intensify large-scale mining, resource extraction, and data center development, resulting in environmental destruction and the displacement of Indigenous Peoples and farmers.”

Meanwhile, youth leaders from the United Church of Christ in the Philippines—Middle Luzon Jurisdictional Area Christian Youth Fellowship (UCCP MLJA-CYF) echoed this call in a manifesto titled “Kapayapaang Para sa Sangnilikha, Hindi Para sa Imperyalistang Bansa!” and warned that communities in Central Luzon will bear the brunt of the project’s ecological and social costs. “While we recognize the importance of technological and economic development, such progress must never come at the expense of Philippine sovereignty, the welfare of the people, the protection of creation, the rights of Indigenous Peoples on the margins, and peace not only in Luzon but across the entire Philippines… What we are fighting for is engagement and trade grounded in equality, respect for sovereignty, and mutual benefit—not the domination of a few and entanglement in conflicts that should never become the burden of the Filipino people.”

Caritas Philippines president and San Carlos Bishop Gerardo Alminaza said in August that the proposed Tarlac development zone directly threatens Indigenous communities and vital local resources. “The site is not empty land. It is home to Aeta Indigenous families, farmers, and rural communities whose rights and livelihoods must come before corporate and geopolitical interests. Pax Silica must not become another pretext for land conversion, displacement, destructive mining, or the diversion of electricity and water away from public needs.”

Catholic Bishops’ Conference of the Philippines (CBCP) President Cardinal Pablo Virgilio David urged authorities to prove that the project serves ordinary citizens rather than foreign strategic agendas. “The real question is whether it will help build what Pope Leo calls a civilization of love rather than a culture of power—a future in which technological progress serves human dignity, social fraternity, care for our common home, and peace among nations.”

Seven bishops of the Ecumenical Bishops Forum (EBF) issued a joint pastoral statement warning that Pax Silica undermines human dignity, workers’ rights, and national sovereignty. The forum includes the UCCP, Iglesia Filipina Independiente, United Methodist Church, Episcopal Church in the Philippines, and Roman Catholic Bishop Emeritus Deogracias Iñiguez Jr.

Bayombong Bishop Jose Elmer Mangalinao urged citizens to actively oppose the Capas hub due to its links to large-scale mining and environmental destruction. Meanwhile, the Catholic Educational Association of the Philippines (CEAP) and Church People-Workers Solidarity (CWS) pressed for full public disclosure and a transparent national dialogue on the agreement’s impact on workers and communities.

As progressive networks including the Promotion of Church People’s Response (PCPR) and the Student Christian Movement of the Philippines (SCMP) continue to mobilize rapid-response relief and vigils for those jailed in Taguig, faith advocates maintain that standing with displaced farmers, workers, and detained protesters remains central to their prophetic witness. (DAA)

title: Int’l groups condemn police brutality
content:
Police officers forcibly grab human rights activists and multisectoral leaders during a protest in Cebu City on November 16, 2026. Screengrab from Bulatlat's video

By Dominic Gutoman and Anne Marxze Umil

International groups denounced the police brutality on November 15, the first day of the 49th ASEAN Summit.

In a statement, the International Association of Democratic Lawyers (IADL) expressed strong condemnation over the violent dispersal and mass arrests of the activists.

They said that instead of arresting international offenders like Sen. Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa who has an outstanding International Criminal Court warrant, “the Philippine police and military are using their superior force to harass and arrest peaceful demonstrators and protestors and to stifle dissent and lawful redress of grievances.”

The group stressed that the police brutality and mass arrests are overkill, violating the Philippine Constitution and the country’s laws in the presence of ASEAN member-states, other heads of state, and the United Nations Secretary General.

“The IADL in particular is holding the police Chief PGen Jose Melencio Nartatez, Jr., Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla, and President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. himself as well as identified individual members of security forces responsible,” the group said in a statement.

The events of the 49th ASEAN Summit happen at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City until November 18, bringing leaders from 11 member-states and representatives of nine dialogue partner-countries.

The Asia Pacific Forum on Women Law and Development (APWLD) stressed that police brutality and state-sanctioned harassment are blatant attacks on fundamental rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly which violates Articles 19 and 21 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR).

“The Philippine government’s actions also violate their international obligations under the UN Declaration on Human Rights Defenders and the UN General Assembly resolution which calls upon all States to take concrete measures to protect human rights defenders and recognise the vital work they do,” APWLD said in a statement. “We call on the international community, civil society organisations and feminist movements across Asia and the Pacific to amplify their demands, release statements of solidarity and support ongoing legal and humanitarian aid for those detained.”

In a press conference on November 16, Jheri Lising, representative of International League of Peoples’ Struggles (ILPS)-US, said that these arrests are part of a broader pattern of repression against people who stand up to US imperialism and its wars of aggression. “The Philippine government is once again demonstrating its willingness to trample on people’s democratic rights to protect US interests. We stand with the Filipino people in opposing Pax Silica, Trump’s visit, and the continuing US intervention in the Philippines.”

June Colcol of Bagong Alyansang Makabayan-US said that “the Filipino people, including our diaspora, have every reason to oppose Trump’s visit and the US economic and military agenda behind it.”

Colcol said that Pax Silica serves US strategic interests, deepens the Philippines’ dependence on foreign capital and technology, and offers no real path to national development. “The Marcos government will not silence us for exposing this agenda. We will not allow these mass arrests to set the tone for the international week of action. We remain indignant and determined to push through with our planned actions and mobilizations, in the Philippines and around the world.”

Arnold Padilla, secretary general of ILPS-Philippines said that the Marcos government will not succeed in silencing them.

“We will not allow yesterday’s arrests to dictate the course of this international week of action. We remain indignant, and we will push through with our plans to expose and oppose the agenda of Trump and Marcos. The demand for accountability will continue to be heard in the streets of the Philippines and across the world,” Padilla said. (DAA)

author: Chantal Eco
title: Will the new FPIC guidelines fast-track the Pax Silica hub in ancestral lands?
content:
Indigenous Aytas from different villages in Capas, Tarlac, listen to an environmental advocate during a community gathering on August 16, 2026, to discuss the impacts of the proposed Pax Silica hub on their land. Photo by Chantal Eco / Bulatlat

“It was really built to cater to corporations. Any semblance that it protects IP rights and allows Indigenous peoples to say no is gone.”

Mandor Matias, 45, has lived all his life on his family’s land in Sitio Binyayan in Capas, Tarlac. He and his relatives plant rice and vegetables on about three hectares of land. But on July 15, employees from the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) came to his house. They pointed to the planted land in front of it, handed him a paper to sign and offered P30 (USD 0.47) per square meter, or about P900,000 (US$ 14,100) for all three hectares.

“They gave me a paper and asked me to sign it. I said I didn’t need to sign it. If I signed it, it would be as if I had accepted payment,” Matias told Bulatlat in Filipino.

He was not told why they were being pushed to sell their land. He later learned through social media and then confirmed by their village head, that the Pax Silica hub, a U.S.-backed hub for artificial intelligence and semiconductor manufacturing, will be built on their land.

Matias is an indigenous Ayta. His home and farm now lie within the area of the proposed Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park, a 1,620-hectare hub in New Clark City that the BCDA is developing with the United States under the Pax Silica framework. Their fate may now be decided under new consent rules. In May, the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) approved the contentious amendments to the guidelines on free, prior and informed consent (FPIC), and a copy was only released publicly in September. The 2026 guidelines shorten deadlines, approve permits automatically when officials fail to act on time, and let some government projects pass with a document review instead of a full community vote. Indigenous groups warn the rules could clear the way for Pax Silica and other “development projects” on ancestral lands.

The FPIC process could take months to years, especially when a project could greatly affect the ancestral land and the community is divided. The new FPIC guidelines run on tight deadlines: seven working days for the NCIP’s field investigation, 10 days for community assemblies on large projects and up to 60 days for the community to decide. If NCIP officials fail to act on time on a completed consent report, the certificate is issued automatically.

Government-funded projects need only a document review if they are “non-commercial.” Those with private partners or long-term impacts go to Category A or B, as the regional director decides. Projects that displace residents fall under Category A, the strictest track. But a project can get its certificate even before it is clear which households will be affected. Protections for those families can be settled later. Meanwhile, even after a community says no, the applicant keeps the right to refile.

Funa-ay Claver, an Indigenous youth leader and spokesperson of Katribu, said the BCDA may avoid FPIC altogether by insisting that no Indigenous people live on the site.

“It was really built to cater to corporations. Any semblance that it protects IP rights and allows Indigenous peoples to say no is gone,” Claver explained in Filipino.

She said the categories depend on a project’s scale, not on how many people it affects, and that manufacturing hubs are not mentioned anywhere. She added that the NCIP never released a draft for public comment.

Katribu said it is wary of even calling on the BCDA to “uphold FPIC.” Under the new rules, Claver said, consent risks becoming a checklist that only clears the way for the project.

At a media forum of the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines (FOCAP) in September, BCDA President Joshua Bingcang claimed that they have always consulted communities whenever there’s a project or development within New Clark City. While showing pictures of what he described as consultations, he did not specifically say that they have already consulted, much less secured the consent of the Aytas living in the area where the Pax Silica hub will be built.

He called the hub site “already BCDA property” and promised, “We will not just kick them out… there will be consultations.”

Trade Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo, who was on the panel, said the site’s irregular boundary was drawn so the land is “already free of any communities.”

An overlay of the BCDA site on NCIP ancestral domain maps done by Countermapping PH, a group of geographers, shows that part of the site lies within an existing titled ancestral domain and that the entire hub falls inside the Aeta Hungey ancestral domain claim, which has been pending since 1999.

Petronila Muñoz, an Ayta leader, said no one talked to them before the hub was announced.

“No one. They just showed up there. They handed out letters,” she said.

Just two years after the NCIP was created, the Ayta Hungey first filed their ancestral domain claim in 1999, which is now under Certificate of Ancestral Domain Title (CADT) Application No. R03-TAR-002-A. Their ancestral land has yet to be formally recognized.

“What will become of us if we lose our ancestral land?” she asked, naming what is at stake: their church, their burial ground and their livelihood.

Matias say they will not leave their home and their lives and livelihood are rooted in their land.

“How can we leave if we don’t know of any relocation site to move to?” Matias asked.

Muñoz said that their opposition to Pax Silica is not only for them Aytas but for every Filipino because the project will destroy the environment.

“Our love for our ancestral land is equal to our very lives,” Muñoz said.

Matias said he tells his neighbors the same thing. “We just keep fighting. As long as we stay united. Let’s not allow Pax Silica to be built.” (RVO)

content:

Where is the respect for farmers and Aytas who will be evicted from their communities because of Pax Silica?

This is the response of Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) in Malacañang’s recent public statement to “show courtesy” as the Philippines hosts the 49th ASEAN Summit from November 15 to 18.

“We will hold protests before, during, and after the ASEAN Summit and Trump’s visit,” the group said in a statement. US President Donald Trump is expected to arrive in the Philippines next week.

In a press briefing on November 10, Malacañang’s Press Officer Claire Castro appealed to the protesters not to schedule rallies during the arrival of the international delegations and “show the genuine hospitality and good character of the Filipino people.”

“Respect for visitors? How about respect for vendors and urban poor displaced by ‘clearing operations’? Where is the respect for farmers and Aytas who will be evicted from their communities because of Pax Silica?” Bayan asked.

Bayan, together with multi-sectoral groups, launched the 12 days of protest which kicked off on November 4. The group stressed that the Philippine government should not welcome “war criminals and foreign plunderers” like Trump at the expense of the Filipino people’s welfare and their right to protest.

The Philippine National Police increased the number of personnel to more than 23,000, coming from the National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO), Armed Forces of the Philippines, Bureau of Fire Protection, and other concerned agencies.

Human rights group Karapatan described the ASEAN preparations as “over-the-top” and are reminiscent of the huge police deployment during the State of the Nation Address (SONA) last July.

“And we all know how that played out. Fifty-one protesters were arrested even before the protest program began, with many of those arrested taken merely because they wore black,” said Cristina Palabay, secretary-general of Karapatan. “This is our country, and we have every right to protest, especially when the policies and actions of these very visitors threaten our people’s rights and interests. US President Donald Trump is not merely a guest whose presence demands deference. The US is actively intervening in our country’s affairs, advancing its economic and military interests at the expense of Filipino sovereignty and people’s rights.”

The United States leads the Pax Silica Initiative, which plans to establish a 4,000-acre industrial hub within the Philippines’ Luzon Economic Corridor. Described as the first “AI-native industrial acceleration hub,” the proposed site is being positioned as an economic security zone intended to strengthen shared supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors, electronics, and other goods.

Read: ‘Pax Silica’ initiative seen as war production, environment destruction

Progressive groups also assailed the worsening economic situation amid grand preparations for the 49th ASEAN Summit.

Independent think tank group IBON Foundation said that the current low wages failed to keep up with the country’s inflation — climbing up to 7.8 percent in October from 7.2 percent in September. The group stressed that rising prices of these commodities, along with rice, are affecting poor and low income families.

The unemployment in the country also increased by almost 909,000, according to the data of the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), though the IBON Foundation argued that the number could be higher.

The number of unemployed Filipinos has raised the Philippine unemployment rate to 5.4 percent, making it the highest among its Southeast Asian neighbors based on the latest data in Indonesia (4.8%), Malaysia (2.9%), Vietnam (2.2%), Singapore (2%), and Thailand (0.9%).

The Philippines is also performing the poorest in terms of economic performance, compared to its counterparts in Southeast Asia. It has among the lowest GDP growth in the region at 2.1 percent compared to Brunei (0.02%), Thailand (1.9%), Malaysia (5.3%), Singapore (5.4%), Indonesia (5.5%) and Vietnam (10%).

“The government’s business-as-usual approach is worsening joblessness, eroding incomes and making the cost of living soar for millions of Filipinos,” said IBON Foundation, warning the administration of Ferdinand Marcos Jr. that the country is rapidly heading towards stagflation. They called on the government to increase spending on agricultural production, support small enterprises, and boost household purchasing power.

Urban poor group Kalipunan ng Damayang Mahihirap (Kadamay) said in a statement that the rising prices of fuel and basic commodities and the temporary displacement of the informal workers affected by the ASEAN Summit are pushing the Filipino families at greater risk.

“Where will the driver get money to buy food for their family? What budget will vendors make if they have no income? What about their children’s school allowance? No matter how much Marcos Jr. tries to cover it up, he cannot hide the glaring poverty in the country,” said Kadamay secretary-general Mimi Doringo.

The transport group Piston will hold a nationwide strike. Farmers and indigenous groups will also organize camp-outs bringing their issues from the countryside to the city for the ASEAN delegates and Trump to hear.

Karapatan said that they stand in solidarity with the Filipino people “as they courageously assert their legitimate demands in the face of heightened repression.”

“The people will not be silenced or intimidated into surrendering their rights and sovereignty for the sake of the Marcos regime’s hosting of the ASEAN Summit,” Palabay concluded. (RTS, AMU, DAA)

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: Peasant organizer persists despite surveillance
content:
Jesus Monasterial. (Photo from Photo from Tanggol Magsasaka-TK)

Repeated surveillance restricted his movements and caused anxiety over his family’s safety.

When he was a university student, he questioned the purpose of agricultural education. Now he is organizing landless farmers and fisherfolk.

Jesus Monasterial has spent more than two years working with rural communities in Southern Tagalog. However, his work resulted in repeated surveillance by state forces, peasant groups said.

On October 31, Tanggol Magsasaka–Timog Katagalugan reported that a police intelligence operative identified as “Bruno” had been asking about Monasterial’s whereabouts in Lian, Batangas. The operative was reportedly previously assigned in Nasugbu.

At the time, Monasterial was assisting a protest camp in Barangay San Diego, where farmers, fisherfolk, and residents opposed the possible demolition of several houses.

“I was on my way back to the people’s protest camp in San Diego when news reached us that someone had been asking about my personal information,” he said.

The camp was established by Samahang Mangangawil 1979 and the San Diego Homeowners’ Association, with support from the Katipunan ng mga Samahang Magbubukid sa Timog Katagalugan (KASAMA-TK) and Pambansang Lakas ng Kilusang Mamamalakaya ng Pilipinas–Timog Katagalugan (PAMALAKAYA-TK).

The incident prompted fellow organizers to discuss security measures. They also plan to file a complaint before the Commission on Human Rights (CHR).

Monasterial’s involvement in peasant organizing began at the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) where he was enrolled in BS Agricultural Biotechnology.

Coming from a family of farmers in Bicol, where his grandparents worked as agricultural tenants, he became increasingly critical of an agricultural education system that he said served the interests of transnational corporations rather than addressing farmers’ lack of land and government support.

Through the League of Filipino Students–UPLB, he became involved in social issues action and joined community immersions with farmers in Tartaria, Silang, Cavite, as well as Mangyan communities in Mindoro and Dumagat communities in Rizal.

These experiences led him to leave his studies and become a full-time organizer. He now serves as deputy secretary-general of KASAMA-TK.

His work involves staying in communities, conducting consultations and political education, and helping establish local farmers and fisherfolk associations.

“Being a full-time organizer means devoting my entire time to the communities and being far from my loved ones,” he said, adding that he had to set aside his plan to finish college.

The October 31 incident was not the first reported surveillance involving Monasterial.

On July 19, 2026, soldiers from the 16th Infantry Battalion of the Philippine Army reportedly sought to identify the organizers of KASAMA-TK’s Regional Peasant Consultation in Barangay Malinis, Lemery, Batangas.

On September 21, a man introducing himself as “Del” Dela Cruz reportedly approached a member of Sugarfolks’ Unity for Genuine Agricultural Reform (SUGAR-Batangas), attempting to persuade the member to leave the organization and provide information about its activities.

According to Tanggol Magsasaka–Timog Katagalugan, the man showed footage of a protest outside the Department of Agriculture regional office led by the Alyansa ng Magsasaka para sa Kumpensasyon (AMK), SUGAR-Batangas, KAISAHAN, and KASAMA-TK. He allegedly warned the member against working with Monasterial, claiming that the organizer was “already drawing attention.”

The protest resulted in a dialogue with government representatives to demand agricultural inputs and implements for farmers and farmworkers affected by successive calamities.

The groups also cited previous incidents in Barangay Casile, Laguna; Lupang Ramos and Tartaria, Cavite; and Coron, Palawan.

Monasterial said that the repeated surveillance restricted his movements and caused anxiety over his family’s safety. “Repeated surveillance limits my movements as an organizer and makes me fear returning home to my family because they might also be targeted by the state due to my advocacy.”

Despite the threats, Monasterial said that his work remains rooted in the struggles of farmers and farmworkers.

In Batangas, he witnessed sugarcane cutters and loaders receiving only P350 to P400 for every ton of cane harvested and loaded onto trucks. Their wages are paid at the end of harvesting seasons that can last six months, forcing many to rely on loans and advances.

Through community discussions, he helps workers understand their rights to organize unions and demand decent wages, humane working conditions, and genuine land reform.

“I continue organizing despite the threats and dangers because I know that what I am doing is not wrong and is necessary,” he said.

Addressing allegations that he was recruiting farmers, Monasterial acknowledged encouraging them to establish their own organizations. “I am indeed encouraging them to establish their own farmers and fisherfolk associations.”

“People naturally resist a society where farmers have no land, yet land is reserved for foreigners, and those who produce the country’s food have nothing to eat,” he said.

Citing figures from their organization, Monasterial said that 56 of the 72 political prisoners in Southern Tagalog come from farming and indigenous communities or are their advocates.

Tanggol Magsasaka–Timog Katagalugan called on allied organizations to condemn the surveillance and urged the CHR and the local government of Lian to investigate the incident and protect the rights of Monasterial and the affected residents.

Monasterial also called for accountability for human rights violations, the repeal of the Anti-Terrorism Act, and the abolition of the National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC).

For Monasterial, organizing is essential for farmers and fisherfolk confronting landlessness, displacement, and the loss of their livelihoods. Despite the surveillance, he stressed that their right to organize and defend their communities must be protected. (RTS, DAA)

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Rights groups support proposed treaty on crimes against humanity
content:
Photo by Raymund B. Villanueva/Kodao Productions

Philippine-based and international human rights groups called for the adoption of the proposed Crimes Against Humanity Convention to provide more avenues for victim-survivors and strengthen accountability mechanisms against high-level perpetrators, governments, and corporations.

Crimes against humanity is the only core international crime without a dedicated treaty on prevention, punishment, and inter-state cooperation. The only international legal remedy available for the victims-survivors is the prosecution of the International Criminal Court (ICC), which is currently facing consecutive sanctions from the Donald Trump administration of the United States.

Read: US intensifies sanctions vs. ICC

The proposal of the Crimes Against Humanity Convention is one of the topics that takes center stage during the ASEAN Civil Society Conference in the Philippines this year, October 27 to 29, 2026, weeks before the official summit.

“Victims and survivors of human rights violations, wars, and genocide must have more avenues to pursue justice and accountability,” Karapatan Secretary General Cristina Palabay told Bulatlat.

Crimes against humanity are defined by the Rome Statute as acts committed as part of a widespread or systemic attack directed against any civilian population, with knowledge of the attack. This includes, but not limited to murder, extermination, enslavement, deportation or forcible transfer of population

Palabay said that the Convention is of utmost significance, especially in the quest for justice of families and communities affected by widespread extrajudicial killings during the administration of Rodrigo Duterte, who is now in ICC custody, awaiting trial starting on November 30.

The Prosecution is expected to present some witnesses, followed by the observations of the Common Legal Representative of the Victims. The Defense (Duterte’s counsel) will also have the opportunity to present its case and witnesses.

Duterte is charged with three counts of crimes against humanity — extrajudicial killings when he was the mayor of Davao City from 2013 to 2016 (Davao Death Squad killings), murder of ‘high-value targets’ across the Philippines, and the murder and attempted murder cases during the barangay clearance operations when he was President (‘Oplan Tokhang’ killings).

Rights groups monitored more than 30,000 extrajudicial killing victims of Duterte’s anti-illegal drugs campaign, which is significantly higher than the official government records of over 6,000 victims. Only five cases resulted in conviction and some of them remain on appeal.

During the ASEAN CSO conference, Jerrie Abella, Amnesty International’s regional campaigner, said that the prosecution of the perpetrator of crimes against humanity brings hope to the families of extrajudicial killings under Duterte’s so-called “drug war”.

“A mother took a long time to muster the courage to talk about her loss and to actively fight for justice. Inspired and empowered not just by the support that her newfound community offered, but also by the fact that Duterte is now in jail and awaiting trial,” said Abella.

“This is just one of the more tangible results of prosecuting an alleged perpetrator of crimes against humanity, even as we may still be years away from the actual court decision,” he added.

However, Abella enumerated several critical gaps for the accountability of the perpetrators and full justice, including Duterte’s co-perpetrators who remain free and are hiding, the national judicial system’s failure to prosecute perpetrators with only a handful of police officers convicted, and the failure of the government to prevent the crime from happening in the first place.

“Impunity persists precisely because the system we have in place allows it,” Abella said. “With this Convention, states will be obligated not just to investigate and prosecute these crimes, but also to adopt concrete measures to prevent their commission.”

A key recommendation from Amnesty International is to recognize the survivors’ right to truth in the context that disinformation happens during the anti-drug campaign until the present administration when coordinated online attacks against victims and their families have intensified.

Read: Women human rights defenders face rising tech-assisted violence

The Convention is not only relevant for the Philippines but for all countries, especially in Asia like Palestine, Myanmar, Cambodia, Indonesia, and Timor-Leste, among others.

Asia Justice Coalition, an international human rights organization campaigning for the Crimes Against Humanity Convention in the region, mapped the position of Asian states based on the submission of member countries in the United Nations and the Sixth Committee Session in October 2026. The Philippines is one of the countries with a positive position.

“We do not have a regional court, we do not have regional units coming. And therefore, I think it will be an important step for us to advocate for such conventions,” said Aakash Chandran, senior law and advocacy manager of AJC.

With the adoption of the Crimes Against Humanity Convention, states will be able to prosecute, not only individuals, but also companies who are engaged in facilitating the crime. Since prevention is a novel aspect of the treaty, the victims’ right to truth mandates states to prevent disinformation against victims and regulate companies like Meta.

The Draft Articles, created by the United Nations International Law Commission, stipulated that the treaty will not create a court, but enable inter-states cooperation for the investigation and prosecution of perpetrators, complimenting the ICC. Jan Wetzel, Senior Policy Advisor of Amnesty International, makes fugitive-Senator Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa as an example, saying that if he is found in Thailand, the country would have to investigate, arrest, potentially try, or extradite him.

“If any country finds a suspect of crimes against humanity in their territory, they need to arrest that person. They need to make an initial investigation: they must try or hand them over to somewhere else to be tried. This is the global community responding,” Wetzel said.

The ICC can only address the individual criminal responsibility, leaving the state responsibility for the crimes against humanity aside. With the treaty, the states can be held accountable by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) for its failure to adequately prevent and/or punish the crimes that occur within their territory.

The Philippines assumes the ASEAN chairship this year. The country will be hosting the 49th ASEAN Summit from November 16 to 18, 2026, with more than 10,000 expected delegates from various countries.

Filipino progressive groups launched 12 days of protest ahead of the summit and the visit of United States President Donald Trump, whom they accuse to be a human rights violator and the brainchild of the Pax Silica initiative.

Read: Trump out! | Progressive groups launch 12 days of protest

“Soon they [Trump administration] will come down hard because this is everything that they’re against,” said Weltzer. “So at some point, they will discover us and they will start actively working against this, which has a practical implication since all negotiations happen in New York.”

The Trump administration has previously sanctioned 13 prosecutors and judges of the ICC, three Palestinian human rights organizations, and the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory Francesca Albanese. The sanctions escalated after the ICC looked into war crimes committed by US troops in Afghanistan in 2018 up to the ongoing genocide of the U.S. and Israel in Palestine.

He added, “We know by now that access to New York is getting more and more limited, not just because of costs but also of visa restrictions. Organizations like us, if you work with the ICC, maybe you cannot come in because it is under sanctions. Even [United Nations] special rapporteurs cannot come in. The space is getting smaller, which is why we call for regional consultations.”

The treaty negotiations will start in 2028 on the basis of the draft articles. The Preparatory Committee for the Convention already started its meeting this January 2026. Their second session is scheduled in April 2027 to discuss rules of procedure, stakeholder participation including civil society, and finalization of the compiled text for the official negotiations. (RTS, RVO)

title: The thrill of group bike rides
content:
Bikers have been bonded by the daily commute or the frequent group rides, and this ritual of biking together can be turned into an advocacy action. This should not be a surprise since the tribe of bikers who regularly ride together suffers from the same grave inefficiencies that plague our roads and communities.

Biking brings calm and exhilaration at the same time, and these feelings are amplified during a group ride.

Planning a group ride takes time and patience, and it is deservedly celebrated when it happens.

It is usually done for leisure, a chill time with fellow bikers. It can be a training session for a scheduled race. Or it can become the power of many if organized to promote a cause.

Whatever the intent that pedals the ride, it is necessary to have trust, coordination, and the unity to move forward in one direction.

Safety measures are learned, relearned, enforced, and adopted during the ride. Newbies take cues from fellow riders, hand signals are introduced, and road rules that apply to cyclists are highlighted in real time. The grounding experience allows bikers to map out routes, rediscover a place from a new perspective, and become familiar with the local scenery. title: Farmers, fisherfolk demand urgent aid amid El Niño, rising fuel prices
content:
The absence of reliable irrigation makes it difficult for farmers to continue planting during periods of extreme heat.







By Wendyl Geronimo

Davao Today




From drought-stricken farms in Davao and Nueva Ecija to fishing communities in Albay, farmers and fisherfolk are demanding government assistance, protection against land grabbing and genuine agrarian reform as El Niño, mounting production costs and development projects threaten their livelihoods.




Amid worsening agricultural conditions, rising production expenses and continuing disputes over land ownership, farmers and fisherfolk across the Philippines are calling for immediate government intervention, warning that insufficient assistance and threats of displacement are pushing rural communities deeper into poverty.




Their demands come as agricultural communities confront the effects of El Niño, inadequate irrigation systems, expensive fuel and fertilizer, and development projects that farmers organizations say threaten thousands of hectares of farmland.




In the Davao Region, prolonged dry conditions have affected agricultural production, particularly among farmers dependent on rainfall.

title: Thousands of farmlands in Bicol converted to mining, energy, infra projects
content:
Claiming the Land: Kilusang Magbubukid ng Bicol provides assistance to affected farmers and members of the local peasant group in Bula, Camarines Sur. (Photo By Reynard Magtoto/Bulatlat)

Farmers organizations warned that agricultural land conversion and large-scale development projects could displace farming communities, threaten food production and undermine farmers’ access to land.

Farmers organizations in the Bicol region have raised concerns over alleged land grabbing and agricultural land conversion involving haciendas, mining operations, renewable energy developments and infrastructure projects.

The farmers travelled to Manila late in October to call on the Marcos Jr. administration to stop land grabbing and land-use conversion of agricultural lands.

In Camarines Norte, peasant groups identified 25,000 hectares associated with the Mabilo Copper-Gold Project, while another 64,884 hectares were linked to a renewable energy development in Mount Labo.

An additional 321 hectares were identified in connection with mining operations in the province.

In Albay, the organizations identified several disputed landholdings, including 141 hectares at Hacienda Mitra/Illas in Guinobatan, 130 hectares at Hacienda Alsua in Pio Duran, 250 hectares at Hacienda Asistio in Ligao, and 200 hectares at Hacienda Ribaya, also in Ligao.

content:

For ILPS Philippines, these agreements are not merely defense arrangements. They further integrate the country into Washington’s military operations and its First Island Chain strategy against China.

The arrival of US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth in Cebu on October 28 has drawn condemnation from progressive groups, which warned that the Philippines is increasingly being drawn into Washington’s military and economic agenda at the expense of national sovereignty.

The International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines said Hegseth’s visit for the ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting comes amid the Trump administration’s aggressive expansion of US military power in the Asia-Pacific and its preparations for greater confrontation with China.

The group described Hegseth as a key enforcer of Washington’s war agenda, criticizing Ferdinand Marcos Jr. administration for facilitating the growing US military presence in the country.

Under the Marcos administration, military cooperation between Manila and Washington has expanded through weapons deployments, joint military exercises, intelligence-sharing arrangements, and the increased use of Philippine military facilities.

Trigger warning: details of violence and death

Nine years after their son was killed in former president Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Nanette and Bong Castillo stepped forward to the Truth Commission’s fifth Public Truth-Telling Session on October 23 to recount what they believe happened to Aldrin Castillo and seek answers on his death.

They believe that the case of their son may have been a case of mistaken-identity, while the police and medical records reviewed by forensic pathologist Raquel Fortun exposed significant gaps in the original documentation of Aldrin’s death.

Aldrin was 32 when gunmen shot him in Tondo, Manila, on October 2, 2017. He was visiting his sister to help repair her air conditioner.

A significant part of the ruling concerned the Strengthening Assistance for Government Infrastructure and Social Programs (SAGIP).

The Supreme Court’s (SC) declaration that the 2024 and 2025 national budgets were unconstitutional has renewed calls to hold Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and other government officials accountable for the flood control corruption scandal. This also exposes how budget insertions and discretionary funds enabled the questionable use of billions of pesos in public money.

In its October 7 ruling on Lagman v. Congress (G.R. No. 271059), the high court struck down budgetary additions that exceeded the spending ceiling submitted by the President. It also permanently prohibited the release mechanisms for certain Unprogrammed Appropriations (UA) under the 2026 national budget.

title: Cyberlibel complaints vs journalists strengthen calls to decriminalize libel
content:
The criminal sanction for Philippine libel laws is “excessive” and is in violation of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) to which the Philippines is a signatory.

Libel complaints were recently filed against journalists and media company executives. For a journalists’ group, these validate the previous calls to decriminalize libel.

The GMA chapter of the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) stressed that libel laws silence journalism. “[C]riminalizing speech only undermines the public’s fundamental right to know,” the chapter said in a statement.

Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo Duterte filed libel and cyberlibel complaints against GMA executives and broadcast journalists which stemmed from the network’s report about alleged cash deliveries to the Dutertes claimed by dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.

Duterte filed the complaint before the Davao City Prosecutor’s Office on October 23, more than two weeks after his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, made a joke about filing a multimillion-peso libel case against GMA Network. Her remarks happened during a press conference on October 6 while reading her affidavit which answers Gracioso’s claims.

title: Proposed foreign-funded wind projects threaten Bicol fishers
content:
Photo frrom Province of Camarines Sur

“If they say this project is for development, development for whom? This is not for us fisherfolk.”

Norberto Tobias of Tanggol San Miguel Bay (SMB) Network stressed this point as he and other fisherfolk from Bicol expressed opposition to the planned 1,000-megawatt San Miguel Bay Offshore Wind Farm.

They joined the Kampuhang Magbubukid (peasant camp) in front of the Department of Agrarian Reform from October 15 to 20.

The proposed wind farm covers 23,307 hectares of coastal waters across municipalities in Camarines Sur and Camarines Norte, including the fishing communities in Calabanga, Cabusao, Tinambac, Siruma, Sipocot, Basud, and Mercedes. This affects at least 6,000 small-scale fisherfolk.

Tobias said in a statement that the planned wind project is only for the profit of foreign companies and its local partner.

The project reportedly started its pre-development phase in 2023 but the fisherfolk communities countered that they only learned about it in 2025.
